opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
Today's readings left me with more questions than answers.

Jeremiah is lamenting over Israel. The kingdom is falling. The people have turned away from God. There is famine, suffering, death, and he cries out, "Have you utterly rejected Judah?" It is painful to read because it sounds like someone who knows God but cannot understand why He seems so far away.

I understand that feeling.

Lately, our life has felt heavy. We have lost clients. We asked one client for feedback because we genuinely wanted to know what we could have done better, but she never responded. We leave conversations wondering if we are failing. We question our business, our decisions, our communication, even our identity. It is exhausting.

My prayer this morning was simple. I asked God to release me from my offenses. There are so many. The judgments I make toward my husband when I think he handled something poorly. The endless maneuvering I do to avoid conflict. The overthinking. Wondering whether I am worthy of His mercy while asking for it. Then I read Psalm 98:

*"May your compassion quickly come to us, for we are brought very low."*

That was my prayer before I even knew it. I read Jeremiah and wonder what it must have been like to spend a lifetime warning people who would not listen. Today we do not have prophets standing in the streets calling a nation to repentance. We have the Word of God. We have Christ. Yet suffering remains. Human hearts remain the battlefield.

Sometimes I ask why God seemed so visible then but feels so quiet now. Why don't we hear His voice the way they did? Why does He feel so far away when I am looking for Him every day? Then I realized something I had not considered. Maybe I have been looking for God in changed circumstances instead of a changed heart. Somewhere along the way I began believing that if I sincerely followed Him, if I prayed enough, tried hard enough, loved enough, then life should become easier. The business should settle down. Relationships should improve. Decisions should become obvious.

But Jesus never promised a weed-free field.

In today's Gospel, He says the wheat and the weeds grow together until the harvest. He does not remove every hardship. He does not promise that faithful people will be spared conflict, disappointment, misunderstanding, or grief. He promises that He remains Lord of the field.

That changes everything.

It means the weeds are not proof that He has abandoned us. The struggle is not evidence of His absence.
The relationship with God is often found in the middle of remorse, difficult decisions, conflict, repentance, forgiveness, and choosing charity when resentment feels easier. That is where I meet Him most honestly.

I think many of us spend our lives asking God to remove the weeds while He is teaching us how to remain rooted among them. We all drink the same water. We all carry burdens no one else fully sees. Some are grieving a marriage. Others a child. Some are carrying financial uncertainty. Some are lonely. Some are sick. Some quietly wonder if God has forgotten them because life has become so difficult.

If that is where you are today, I simply want you to know that I believe He has not abandoned us.

Not because life suddenly becomes easier.
Not because every prayer is answered the way we hoped.
But because He has already entered our suffering.

Jeremiah cried out in sorrow. The Psalm cries out for compassion. Jesus Himself entered the field filled with weeds. God did not remain distant from suffering. He walked into it.  Today I still have questions. I still do not know how some things will turn out. I still ask Him to direct my steps because I know how easily my own heart wanders.  But perhaps faith is not hearing every answer. Perhaps faith is continuing to look toward Him when I cannot yet see what He is doing.

If you are hurting today, know this: you are not walking through the field alone.

He is here.

And He has not abandoned us.
